section_1.title: Prerequisites: The Plane-Cone Intersection
section_1.content: Briefly define a double-napped cone and a cutting plane. Visualize how varying the angle of the plane relative to the cone's axis generates circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas.
section_1.example: An animation showing a flat blade slicing through a 3D ice cream cone at different angles to reveal 2D cross-sections.

section_2.title: Introducing Dandelin Spheres
section_2.content: Introduce the 'Dandelin Spheres' as the geometric bridge. Explain that these are imaginary spheres tucked inside the cone, tangent to both the cone (along a circle) and the cutting plane (at a single point).
section_2.example: A 3D model of a transparent cone containing a glowing sphere that perfectly touches the inner surface and the cutting plane at a single point F.

section_3.title: Connecting the Dots: The Ellipse Proof
section_3.content: Explain that the points of tangency between the spheres and the plane are the 'foci' of the conic section. Show that the sum of distances from any point on the ellipse to the two foci is constant (equal to the distance between the two circles of tangency).
section_3.example: Two squirrels at points F1 and F2 (the foci) on the cutting plane, showing that a thread stretched from one to the other via a point on the ellipse remains constant in length.

section_4.title: Generalization and Conclusion
section_4.content: Extend the logic: explain that for parabolas and hyperbolas, the setup changes slightly (one sphere or different sphere placements), but the tangency principle remains the fundamental 'key' to why these shapes behave the way they do.
section_4.example: A fast-paced visual morphing: showing how shifting the plane until it is parallel to the cone's side turns an ellipse into a parabola.
